name: CI/CD & Pipelines
description: Continuous integration, deployment strategies, pipeline design, artefacts and release safety.

modules.name: CI, CD and Pipeline Design
modules.description: What the terms mean, and what a good pipeline actually does.

cards.prompt: Distinguish continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment.
cards.answer: CI: everyone merges to trunk frequently and every merge is built and tested. Continuous delivery: every green build is *releasable* and deployment is a button. Continuous deployment: every green build ships to production automatically.
cards.explanation: CI is a team practice, not a tool — running Jenkins while sitting on week-old branches is not CI. The prerequisite for the last step is confidence: fast reliable tests, feature flags, monitoring, and a rollback that works.

cards.prompt: What stages belong in a solid pipeline, and in what order?
cards.answer: Lint and type-check → unit tests → build once and produce an immutable artefact → integration tests → security scans (SCA/SAST) → deploy to staging → smoke and end-to-end tests → deploy to production → post-deploy verification.
cards.explanation: Two rules matter most: fail fast (cheapest checks first) and build once, promote the same artefact through every environment. Rebuilding per environment means the thing you tested is not the thing you shipped.

cards.prompt: Why should configuration differ per environment while the artefact does not?
cards.answer: So the binary or image tested in staging is byte-identical to the one in production. Environment differences live in injected configuration and secrets, never in a rebuild.
cards.explanation: This is why images are tagged by commit SHA rather than `latest`, and promoted by re-tagging. `latest` is unpinnable, unrollbackable and non-reproducible — the single most common source of 'it worked yesterday'.

cards.prompt: Your pipeline fails randomly about 10% of the time. Why is that worse than it sounds?
cards.answer: Flaky tests destroy the signal: people re-run until green, so real failures get ignored too. Quarantine flaky tests immediately, track them as bugs, and fix the root cause — usually timing, shared state, ordering or real concurrency bugs.
cards.explanation: A 10% flake rate across 20 independent jobs means most runs fail somewhere. Automatic retries hide the symptom and let it spread. Note that a flaky test sometimes indicates a genuine race in the product — the test is right and the code is wrong.

cards.prompt: How should a pipeline handle secrets and credentials?
cards.answer: Short-lived credentials via OIDC federation instead of stored long-lived keys; secrets scoped per environment; masked in logs; never exposed to workflows triggered by untrusted forks; and least-privilege tokens per job.
cards.explanation: CI is a high-value target — it can push to production and holds every credential. Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA, since a mutable tag lets a compromised action run in your pipeline with your secrets.

modules.name: Deployment Strategies
modules.description: Getting changes into production without taking it down.

cards.answer: Blue-green switches all traffic between two complete environments; canary shifts a small percentage first and increases it while watching metrics.

left.title: Blue-green
points: All users hit the new version at once

right.title: Canary
points: Blast radius limited to a few percent
Needs traffic routing and good telemetry

cards.explanation: Rolling updates are the default in Kubernetes and sit between the two. Whichever you pick, the database is the hard part: schema changes must be backwards compatible so old and new code can run simultaneously.

cards.prompt: How do feature flags decouple deploy from release, and what is the cost?
cards.answer: Code ships dark and is enabled per user, percentage or environment — so a bad feature is switched off without a redeploy. The cost is complexity: every flag doubles the paths through your system, and stale flags rot.
cards.explanation: Treat flags as inventory with an owner and an expiry date. Test the on and off paths. Kill switches for risky dependencies are the highest-value flags; long-lived permanent flags usually mean a configuration option in disguise.

cards.prompt: A deploy is causing errors. Roll back or fix forward?
cards.answer: Roll back first, diagnose after — unless the change included an irreversible migration, in which case fix forward. The decision must be made before the incident, and rollback must be practised.
cards.explanation: This is why migrations are expand/contract: never drop a column in the same release that stops writing it. An untested rollback is not a rollback; rehearse it in staging, and know how long it takes.

cards.answer: Git holds the declarative desired state of the system, and an in-cluster agent (Argo CD, Flux) continuously reconciles the cluster toward it. Deployments happen by merging, not by running commands.
cards.explanation: The wins are a full audit trail, review on infrastructure changes, drift detection and revert-by-git. The trap is secrets — they cannot sit in plain git, so you need sealed secrets, SOPS or an external secrets operator.
